description:
Universal Kaji (fire in japanese 火事) department is a team focused on data analysis, big data and machine learning.

We chose the harmonization between MODIS and VIIRS hotspots data because it's the most fitting to our main area of knowledge and because we felt like this challenge was one of the most worth to solve as it is gonna give a lot of useful information, research and data for all the scientists, emergency responders and firefighters which will help in their respective fields a lot.
summary:
Kaji Hotspot Atlas: a harmonized MODIS + VIIRS burning record, 2000 to today. 

MODIS has observed fires since 2000 but is near the end of its life, while VIIRS detects many more, smaller fires at 375 m. Their records cannot be compared directly. I built a single, sensor-independent series so the focus moves to patterns, trends and anomalies.

Data: I used the full FIRMS archive for the whole planet: MODIS (Terra, Aqua) and VIIRS (S-NPP, NOAA-20, NOAA-21). That’s about 50 GB of CSV and 661 M detections, which I converted into one deduplicated, partitioned Parquet table (10.8 GB) queried with DuckDB.

Data Harmonization:
- Aqua and S-NPP share the same overpass time, so I calibrated Aqua against S-NPP on a 0.25° grid by month, using separate day/night LightGBM Poisson models.
- I trained on 2012–2019 and validated on 2020–2021, right before the satellites’ orbital drift. Validation error: WAPE 0.225, bias −2.8 %.
- Terra fills 2000–2002 through a Terra→Aqua model.
- NOAA-20/21 fill the months where S-NPP has missing days, scaled to S-NPP.
- Near-real-time detections have no FIRMS type, so it is inferred from each location’s history, and the app always flags it.

Web app.
- A world map with a timeline to explore any day since 2000, with filters.
- A by-country view.
- A burning calendar (years × months) for any area.
- Anomalies against the historical median.
- CSV downloads.
Colour-blind-safe colour ramps throughout.
details:
GitHub repo: https://github.com/Motama14/kaji_department

Kaji Hotspot Atlas joins 26 years of satellite fire detections into one consistent record. It covers November 2000 to November 2026, with more than 600 millions active-fire hot spots from five differente satellites with two different sensors:
- Modis on Terra and Aqua
- VIIRS on Suomi NPP, NOAA-20 and NOAA-21
A web app sits on top of the harmonized record so anyone can explore it.

The core problem is that MODIS and VIIRS can't be compared directly. VIIRS has 375M pixels (hotspots), while MODIS has 1km pixels; and to make matters worse VIIRS detects about 6 times more hot spots during the day and about 30 times more at night than Aqua, the satellite that travels over the same paths and time.

This made the data have a 6x jump in 2012 (when VIIRS was oficially deployed) that is about the sensor, not the planet suddenly having more fires; the pipeline removes that jump by:
- Cleaning the data
- Aggregating it: detections are counted on a 0.25º x montly grid, with day and night kept separate
- Calibrating it between Aqua and Suomi NPP using two LightGBM Poisson models (one for day and one for night), using Terra to fill up the two years before Aqua launched and using NOAA-20 to fill up the gaps where S-NPP has no data (it will also carry the data once S-NPP retires since it's younger than NOAA-21)
- Validating: The models were trained on 2012-2019 and tested on 2020-2021, this is because 2021 was the last year before the MODIS orbits started drifting, making the data worse to consider in the validation process.

The web app has two views:
- Interactive map: daily, weekly or montly hot spots on a timeline, with filters, a global view and a by-country view
- Burning calendar: draw an area, enter a bounding box or pick a country, you get a years x months heatmap, the current month compared with its historical median and percentiles, and a CSV download of the points with their source sensor

Intended impact:
The app answers practical questions quickly, the harmonized record already shows useful patterns, about 37% of the world's hot spots occur from July to September, and global fire activity has declined since the early 2000s.

For more information or technicalities check the github repo, thank you for reading.
